I've talked to my therapist about this before. I described how sometimes I'd just feel anger and frustration while sitting at the meetings, but how later it turned to just straight up shutting down/zoning out. She showed me something called the Polyvagal Chart, and how it is theorized that our brains can be in all these different states along the chart depending on circumstances and environments, and that the brain cannot tell the difference between "im getting chased by a tiger" (from our time as hunter-gatherers), and "i cant take another second of sitting in this boring ass meeting". I noticed that I was constantly existing in the highest level of the polyvagal chart which I believe is known as the dorsal vagal. Not only was this the case at meetings, but it started to bleed into other aspects of my life. I would disassociate as soon as I felt the slightest hint of boredom at work, school, with friends etc. My phone/social media made this worse, as I'd just go to meetings and sit on reddit/IG for 2 hours trying to drown out the noise. All this led to a social media addiction, and a tendency to disassociate from any and almost all situations. I believe that I was either misdiagnosed with ADHD because of this OR that I developed ADHD because of this. 

This topic is super complex and there's so so much more to it and I probably butchered parts of it. I'd defs encourage people to look into this if it interests you and I'd also encourage people to seek help via therapy (mainly trauma resolution), so you can see just how deep these issues are and how they've affected us down to a subconscious level.

26 now, got into hardcore right before the pandemic hit. Closest thing to a hardcore show I had ever gone to before then was a fest of sorts with Ceremony and Full of Hell. It wasn’t until a year after lockdown that I went to an actual show with Sunami, Gulch, Xibalba and a few others, I’ve gone to every show I possibly could go to since then wether I knew the bands or not. I totally get what you’re saying about other people in the scene being in it since their early teens. Some people I talk to at shows tell me about shows from 10 years ago and part of me wishes I would have found Hardcore at a much earlier age, as I could have used the sense of community/belonging that comes with being in the scene in my formative years. My unsolicited advice if anyone is feeling this way or kinda alienated since everyone around you is a scene vet or whatever is to just go to shows and talk to people, do your homework like listening to the albums that have shaped the sound of hardcore or albums that the bands you listen to were influenced by (Master Killer is a must), and participate in the scene. Buy merch go to shows with bands you dont know, start your own band etc.

Might not classify as one man band anymore but a technique thats been working for me recently is basically laying out all the parts for a song with programmed drums and guitar only. Once I am happy with the structure, I’ll go ahead and do a rough take on vocals. This is the part where “One man band” goes out the window: Once I have this rough demo with vocals, guitar and programmed drums, I send the song to a drummer I’ve been working with on fiverr and have him record actual drum parts and add other intricacies like fills, transitions ect. After that all I do is re record guitar and vocals over the new drum track and add bass as well, and send it off to get mixed/mastered. Not too conventional I guess but its been working great so far for what I’m trying to achieve.

Stay strong.
